items.title: The Health and Safety (Consultation with Employees) Regulations 1996, regulation 3: Duty of employer to consult
items.quote: the health and safety consequences for those employees of the introduction (including the planning thereof) of new technologies into the workplace
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. Employees not covered by union safety representatives must be consulted 'in good time'. The duty is limited to health and safety; it is the nearest UK statute comes to a duty to consult on new workplace technology. Page shows no known outstanding effects.

items.title: The Safety Representatives and Safety Committees Regulations 1977, regulation 4A: Employer's duty to consult and provide facilities and assistance
items.quote: every employer shall consult safety representatives in good time with regard to
items.why: The matching duty where a recognised union has appointed safety representatives; sub-paragraph (e) covers the introduction, including the planning, of new technologies. Health and safety only.

items.title: The Information and Consultation of Employees Regulations 2004, regulation 20: Standard information and consultation provisions
items.quote: decisions likely to lead to substantial changes in work organisation or in contractual relations
items.why: Shows that informing and consulting are separate duties: information on all three heads, consultation on employment prospects and on these decisions, with a reasoned response and a view to agreement. Applies only where the standard provisions apply (reg. 18). Does not mention AI.

items.title: The Information and Consultation of Employees Regulations 2004, regulation 7: Employee request to negotiate an agreement
items.locator: Reg. 7(2) and (3); Schedule 1 for the 50-employee threshold
items.quote: would result in less than 15 or more than 2,500 employees being required in order for a valid employee request to be made
items.why: Source of the figure. A valid request needs 2% of employees, with a floor of 15 and a ceiling of 2,500. Schedule 1 (read separately at /schedule/1) applies the Regulations to undertakings with 'At least 50' employees from 6 April 2008. An employer may also start negotiations itself (reg. 11).

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: the controller shall seek the views of data subjects or their representatives on the intended processing
items.why: Where a workplace system needs an impact assessment, this is the legal hook for asking workers or their representatives first. Qualified by 'Where appropriate' and by commercial and security interests.

items.title: Employment practices and data protection: monitoring workers. Data protection and monitoring workers
items.locator: Section 'Should we discuss the introduction of monitoring with our workers?'
items.quote: you should seek and document the views of your workers or their representatives (such as trade unions), unless there is a good reason not to
items.why: The regulator's expectation for monitoring tools, including those that infer performance from data. 'Should' is good practice, not a legal requirement. The guidance carries a banner that it is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act. Date given is the page metadata date.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: deployers who are employers shall inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system
items.why: The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page). A duty to inform, not to consult, before a high-risk system is used at work. The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and the text is not yet updated; the brief gives no application date for that reason.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.quote: The board should keep engagement mechanisms under review so that they remain effective.
items.why: The board-level channel for workforce views: a workforce director, an advisory panel or a designated non-executive director, on a comply-or-explain basis. Applies to companies that follow the Code. Says nothing about AI.

items.title: Employment Rights Act 2025, section 29: Collective redundancy: extended application of requirements
items.quote: Subsection (1) applies where an employer is proposing to dismiss as redundant within a period of 90 days or less
items.why: What the 2025 Act changed on consultation: collective redundancy consultation will also be triggered by a threshold number of employees across the employer, not only 20 at one establishment. Notes to section 188 of the 1992 Act show it in force on 6 January 2026 for specified purposes only (S.I. 2026/3). The Act contains no duty to consult on AI.

items.title: My boss the algorithm: an ethical look at algorithms in the workplace
items.quote: Early communication and consultation between employers and employees are the best way to ensure new technology is well implemented and improves workplace outcomes.
items.why: An independent policy paper written for Acas by the Involvement and Participation Association; the page says it is not Acas guidance. Makes the practical case for consulting before introduction. No Acas guidance page on AI at work was found.

items.title: Consulting employees on health and safety: A brief guide to the law (INDG232 rev2)
items.locator: PDF page 3, 'What should consultation with employees involve?'; PDF page 2 for the list of matters, including new technology
items.quote: listening to them and taking account of what they say before making any health and safety decisions
items.why: The regulator's own plain statement of what consultation means under the 1977 and 1996 Regulations already on the list: listening before the decision, not announcing after it. It also lists 'the health and safety consequences of introducing new technology' among the matters and explains 'in good time'. Limits: a short leaflet dated April 2013; health and safety only; says nothing about AI as such.

items.title: Managing technology that manages people: November 2025. A Social Partnership approach to algorithmic management systems in the Welsh public sector
items.publisher: Welsh Government (guidance agreed by the Workforce Partnership Council)
items.locator: Section 'After a new system starts being used'; also 'Before adoption and implementation' and 'Due diligence and consultation during buying or building systems'
items.quote: Feedback from workers and worker representatives should be sought, collected and used to shape the system.
items.why: The only UK government guidance found that sets out consultation on workplace AI step by step: joint audit of existing systems, unions involved in buying or building, an audit framework agreed before use, and feedback used to change the system. It matches the 'feedback tracked and demonstrably considered' and co-design levels. Limits: applies to devolved public sector bodies in Wales only; guidance agreed in social partnership, not law; this page is a summary of longer guidance that was not read (the TUC copy refused access).

items.title: Protection of workers' personal data: An ILO code of practice
items.locator: Section 12, Collective rights, paragraph 12.2(a) and (b) (PDF page 19); paragraph 5.8
items.quote: concerning the introduction or modification of automated systems that process worker's personal data
items.why: International comparator. The ILO code says workers' representatives should be informed and consulted about the introduction or modification of automated systems that process workers' data, and before any electronic monitoring is introduced. It shows the principle is long settled internationally. Limits: published 1997; the code states it has no binding force and only makes recommendations; it predates modern AI.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.locator: Art. 22C(1) and (2)(a) to (d); textual amendment note F1
items.quote: provide the data subject with information about decisions described in paragraph 1 taken in relation to the data subject
items.why: The binding UK rule on telling people about automated decisions taken about them: the employer must have measures that give the worker information about the decision and let them make representations, obtain human intervention and contest it. Limits: it applies only to the automated decisions the Article covers, and to the individual affected, after the decision; it is not a duty to consult the workforce or its representatives before a system goes live. Inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; the page records it as fully in force from 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82).

items.title: Robots, Digitalization, and Worker Voice (GLO Discussion Paper No. 1038)
items.publisher: Filippo Belloc, Gabriel Burdin and Fabio Landini, Global Labor Organization (EconStor repository)
items.quote: Overall, these results cast some doubts on the idea that ER may spur automation by reducing the flexibility of employment relationships.
items.why: Evidence on what worker voice does to technology adoption: across more than 20,000 European establishments, workplaces with employee representation (ER) use robots and advanced digital tools more, not less, and the link runs through influence on training and work organisation. It answers the worry that consulting staff slows adoption. Limits: a discussion paper, not peer reviewed in this version; cross-sectional association plus an Italian case study; about robots and digital tools generally, not AI; it does not measure trust. Parts of the abstract's text layer run words together.

items.title: Advanced Digital Technologies in Unionized Firms
items.publisher: Fabio Berton, Stefano Dughera and Andrea Ricci, Italian Economic Journal (Springer, open access)
items.quote: workplace employee organizations increase the probability of advanced digitalization by around 15 percentage points per year
items.why: Peer-reviewed, open-access study using an instrumental-variable design on a nationally representative survey of Italian firms (2018): workplace employee organisations raise the probability of adopting advanced digital technologies. Supports the case that informing and involving representatives helps new technology land. Limits: Italy only; 2018 data; digital technologies broadly, not AI specifically; measures adoption, not worker trust or outcomes for workers.
